openings.call:chard: Their three Chardonnays are French and Italian, from Domaine des Hâtes Chablis at $110 to Lis Neris Jurosa at $169. A guest who asks for a New World Chardonnay has nothing to order.
openings.call:provrose: Their four rosés come from the Rhône, Languedoc, Campania and Niagara, between $70 and $84, with Montirius La Muse Papilles at $75. A guest asking for a Provence rosé has none to pick.
openings.call:rioja: Their Spanish reds are Fedellos do Couto As Xaras at $153, Envínate Lousas at $173 and Envínate La Santa de Úrsula at $196. A guest asking for Rioja can't order one.
openings.call:amarone: Their Italian reds run from Cocci Grifoni Rosso Piceno at $70 to the Valdicava Brunello Riserva at $820. Nothing is made from dried grapes, so a guest asking for Amarone can't order one.
openings.call:port: Their only sweet wine is Château Nairac Sauternes at $16 for a 2oz glass. A guest who wants a Port after dinner can't order one.
openings.call:icewine: Their only sweet wine is Château Nairac Sauternes at $16 for a 2oz glass. A guest who wants an Ontario Icewine can't order one.
openings.dish:dark: The Chocolate Tart and the Sticky Coffee Pudding are suggested with a Sauternes or a dry wine. Neither is a match for dark, toffee-heavy sweets, and the list has no fortified wine.
openings.ladder:Sparkling:75: Their sparkling goes from Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato at $75 to Tarlant Brut Réserve at $125. A guest who wants Champagne-style bubbles but won't pay $125 has nowhere to land.
openings.glass:local: All five Canadian wines, from Two Sisters and Stratus, are sold by the bottle only. By the glass runs $15 to $23 and none of it is from Ontario.
openings.glass:fizz: Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato at $16 is the only sparkling by the glass. The Champagnes and Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta are sold by the bottle, so a guest who wants a traditional-method glass can't have one.
openings.glass:sweet: Three desserts share one sweet pour, Château Nairac at $16 for 2oz. A table that wants something different with the second dessert has no choice.
openings.call:cab: Their New World Cabernet Sauvignon starts at Crown Point at $460, and Staglin is above it. The nearest everyday choice is Château Camino Salva Haut-Médoc at $84, which is Bordeaux.
openings.mix:Sicily|White: Italy fills 35 of their 76 wines across 11 regions. Feudi di San Gregorio Greco di Tufo at $80 is their southern white, and there is no white from Sicily.
openings.format: They list two large-format bottles, the Paul Jaboulet Aîné Hermitage and the Fontodi Flaccianello. A magnum has a place on the list, but only two are there to choose from.

a-157586.say: You have one sweet wine for three desserts, Château Nairac at $16 for 2oz. A Port at $13 a glass gives the Chocolate Tart and the Sticky Coffee Pudding something that suits them.

story.t: A tawny Port from the Douro, aged in wood. The sheet describes plum, apricot and marmalade, with spice and nutty notes from oak. It is sweet, 20% alcohol, with 104 g/L of sugar.

Port is a name every guest knows, and a tawny is the one people order with dessert or cheese. Ferreira's Doña Antonia is named for a 19th century woman who led the house, which is a one-line story a server can tell.

It is much richer and sweeter than Château Nairac, which is lighter and fresher. Toffee, coffee caramel and chocolate are where it works, because the nutty, dried-fruit character matches them instead of being flattened by them.
They pay $21.10 a bottle and it lands at $70, which is 3.3 times cost. By the glass it is $13 for 2oz, below Nairac's $16, and a bottle gives 12 pours at $1.76 cost each.

dishes.d-chocolate-tart: Dark chocolate with fleur de sel wants a sweet wine with weight. The plum and toffee in a tawny Port sit with the cocoa, and the crème anglaise softens the 20% alcohol.
dishes.d-sticky-coffee-pudding: Walnut, coffee caramel and toffee share the nutty, oxidized notes of a tawny. The Port matches the pudding's sweetness, where a lighter Sauternes would taste thin beside it.

objections.q: "I already have the Nairac for dessert. Why add another sweet wine?"
objections.a: Nairac is listed with the Citrus Parfait, Chocolate Tart and Sticky Coffee Pudding. A Port is a different style, heavier and nuttier, and it gives a table a choice.

objections.q: "Nobody orders Port in a restaurant anymore."
objections.a: I can't prove demand here. At $13 for 2oz it is a small add-on, and a bottle keeps well once opened because of the 20% alcohol.

objections.q: "A 2oz pour at $13 looks small next to the other glasses."
objections.a: It matches how you pour the Nairac at 2oz. Dessert wine is sold in small pours, and $13 sits under Nairac's $16.

a-224766.say: Your sparkling jumps from Serenissima at $75 to Tarlant at $125. This is Ontario traditional-method bubbles landing at $110, and it could be your first Ontario wine by the glass at $21.

story.t: A traditional-method sparkling wine from Niagara-on-the-Lake, at 13.3% alcohol with 12 g/L of sugar. The sheet gives no tasting note. A wine like this is usually crisp and dry, with green apple, citrus and a little brioche, and those flavours are our estimate.
Traditional method means the bubbles form in the bottle, the same way Champagne is made. The guest gets that method from Ontario, with a local name the server can point to on the list.

It is drier and more structured than the Serenissima Prosecco, which is soft and fruity. It is lighter than the Champagnes above it. It suits the Tuna Carpaccio, the Seared Scallop, the Mushroom Parfait and the Caesar.
They pay $32.95 a bottle and it lands at $110, 3.3 times cost. That fits between Serenissima at $75 and Tarlant at $125. By the glass it is $21, five pours a bottle at $6.59 cost each.

dishes.d-tuna-carpaccio: Ponzu and caper want acidity and clean bubbles. This is crisp and dry, and the fizz cuts the eggplant miso. Tarlant is richer and costs $125.
dishes.d-seared-scallop: Crispy pancetta and butter bean are salty and rich, and the bubbles and citrus clean them up. It is a lighter pairing than Bollinger Special Cuvée at $215.
dishes.d-mushroom-parfait: A smooth parfait with pickled shallot needs acid to cut the richness. The crisp bubbles do that, and the brioche note suits the sourdough. It costs well under André Chemin at $140.
dishes.d-burrata-tomato: Burrata is creamy and the tomato and chili oil are sharp. Dry bubbles refresh the mouth between bites. It is a different and cheaper choice than André Chemin Brut Rosé at $142.
dishes.d-caesar-salad: Garlic crouton and parmigiano suit a dry sparkling with citrus. This has less weight than Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta at $126, and it sells for less.

objections.q: "I already have five Champagnes and Franciacorta by the bottle."
objections.a: True, but none is under $125, and none is by the glass. This fills the gap between Serenissima at $75 and Tarlant.

objections.q: "Will guests pay $21 a glass for Ontario sparkling?"
objections.a: The Chablis is $23 by the glass, so $21 is not out of range. If they hesitate, the bottle at $110 is the easier sell.

objections.q: "Five glasses a bottle is not many."
objections.a: Correct, and the cost per pour is $6.59. It works as a sparkling you pour at $21 or sell as a bottle, but it is not a high-volume pour.

a-81653.say: You list three Chardonnays, all French or Italian, from $110 to $169, and no Ontario wine by the glass. This one is Niagara-on-the-Lake, goes on at $75 a bottle and $15 a glass.

story.t: A barrel fermented Chardonnay from Niagara-on-the-Lake, 12% alcohol and 2 g/L sugar, so dry. The sheet gives no tasting note. Our estimate is baked apple, butter and toasty oak, medium-bodied and balanced.

Guests ask for a local glass and Eloise has none, because all five Canadian wines are bottle only. 'Barrel fermented' on the label tells a server it was fermented in oak, which is why it reads richer than an unoaked white. Château des Charmes is a Niagara name the floor can say in one line.

It sits fuller and rounder than Tiefenbrunner Pinot Grigio and Nautilus Sauvignon Blanc, the whites guests pour most by the glass. That weight suits the butter in the Squash Ravioli and the pancetta on the Seared Scallop. It is also softer than the Domaine des Hâtes Chablis at $23 a glass.

They pay $17.95 a bottle, $215.40 for a case of 12. On the list it goes on at $75 and $15 a glass, 4.2 times cost, because their usual 3.4 times would land it under their cheapest bottle. It sits level with Tiefenbrunner Pinot Grigio at $75, just below Two Sisters Riesling at $79. Five glasses a bottle, $3.59 cost a pour.

dishes.d-seared-scallop: Baked apple and butter in the glass meet the sweet scallop and crispy pancetta. Olivier Leflaive Bourgogne Les Sétilles at $150 is leaner. This is the rounder, cheaper pour.
dishes.d-squash-ravioli: Brown butter and toasted pumpkin seed want a wine with some oak and body. The barrel fermented fruit matches the sage and squash. Les Sétilles does the same job at $150.
dishes.d-seared-rainbow-trout: Trout with piquillo pepper and olive is a mild fish that a fuller Chardonnay will not bury. Bianchi Pigato at $157 is more savoury. This one is softer and costs far less.
dishes.d-eloise-wedge-salad: Gorgonzola is rich and salty, and a wine with some weight holds up to it. Antonutti Sauvignon Blanc at $80 is sharper. This one rounds the blue cheese instead of cutting it.
dishes.d-caesar-salad: Garlic crouton and parmigiano are creamy and savoury, which suits oak and butter in the wine. Corda Vermentino at $98 is crisper. This is the fuller, lower-priced alternative.
dishes.d-shrimp-linguine: Lemon, caper and 'nduja give this pasta heat and sharpness. A dry, medium-bodied Chardonnay softens the chili without clashing. Corda Vermentino at $98 is the leaner option.

objections.q: "You've put it at $75 but it costs you $17.95. Isn't that a big lift?"
objections.a: Yes. Their usual multiple would land it under your cheapest bottle, so $75 is the entry price, level with Tiefenbrunner Pinot Grigio. The glass is $15.

objections.q: "I already have Chardonnay from Burgundy. Why add another?"
objections.a: Yours are French and Italian at $110 to $169. A guest asking for a New World or Ontario Chardonnay has nothing to order today.

objections.q: "Will an oaky Chardonnay sell next to my Pinot Grigio and Sauvignon Blanc by the glass?"
objections.a: It is a different style, fuller and rounder, so it would not replace them. Concede the fit is not proven here: it is a new option, not a known seller.

a-353184.say: You list three Spanish reds, all from Ribeira Sacra or the Canary Islands at $153 to $196, and no Rioja. This Riserva goes on at $75 a bottle and $14 a glass.

story.t: A Rioja Classico Riserva at 13.5% alcohol. The sheet gives no tasting note, region or grape. Our estimate is Tempranillo with red cherry, vanilla and leather, medium-bodied and dry.

Rioja is a name guests know and ask for by region. 'Riserva' is a legal term: the wine is aged longer, in oak and in bottle, before release. A server can say that in one line, and it explains the vanilla and leather.

It is softer and warmer than Dissegna Pinot Nero by the glass and lighter than the Haut-Médoc. Medium tannin and fresh acidity make it a food red for roast chicken and the Beef Cheek Pappardelle. It is not built for the Côte de Boeuf.

They pay $21.95 a bottle, $263.40 for a case of 12, 3.4 times cost, their usual. At $75 it sits just below Château Camino Salva Haut-Médoc at $84 and next to Dissegna Pinot Nero at $75. The glass is $14, five pours a bottle, $4.39 cost a pour.

dishes.d-beef-cheek-pappardelle: Braised beef with rosemary wants cherry fruit and some tannin to clear the richness. Rioja Riserva gives both. Travignoli Chianti Rùfina at $70 is brighter and more acidic.
dishes.d-charcoal-roasted-chicken: Guajillo and charred skin suit vanilla and leather from oak ageing. Envínate Lousas at $173 is lighter and more mineral. This is a rounder, much cheaper pour.

objections.q: "I already have two reds at $75 or close to it. Why another?"
objections.a: Dissegna Pinot Nero is $75 and Camino Salva is $84, both French or Italian. None is Rioja, so this answers a request you can't fill.

objections.q: "Stock is only 22 cases. Can you keep me supplied?"
objections.a: It is on consignment and 22 cases is limited. If it sells through, it may not be reordered. Start with it as a listing for the season.

objections.q: "The sheet doesn't even say the grape. How do I explain it?"
objections.a: Fair. Rioja is typically Tempranillo, but we haven't confirmed it from the sheet. Taste it first and describe what is in the glass.

a-317057.say: You list 19 Italian reds and not one Amarone. Masi Costasera would sit at $165, just under Envínate Lousas at $173, and it is the wine to pour beside the grill.

story.t: Masi Costasera is an Amarone from Valpolicella in Veneto, made from Corvina, Rondinella and Molinara. The sheet describes cherry and plum jam with cinnamon and cloves, firm structure, velvety tannins and a marked acidity. At 15% alcohol it is a big wine, and it is dry (our estimate, not the sheet's).

It is heavier and softer than Château Le Crock and Château Camino Salva, which are Bordeaux with firm tannin and less weight. The sheet points it at grilled or roasted red meat and parmesan. That fits the steak and the côte de boeuf. It also works as an after-dinner glass for a guest who skips dessert.

They pay $56.50 a bottle, $678.00 a case of 12. On the list it lands at $165, 2.9 times cost, with $32 by the glass. That sits between Frecciarossa Giorgio Odero Pinot Nero at $163 and Envínate Lousas Viña de Aldea at $173. A bottle is 5 pours, about $11.30 cost a pour. There are 787 cases in the warehouse.

dishes.d-10oz-steak-frites: The peppercorn sauce has heat and fat, and Amarone's dried-fruit weight and firm tannin stand up to both. It is richer and rounder than the Le Crock they pour now.
dishes.d-42oz-cote-de-boeuf: A shared 42oz of grilled beef with a red wine and mustard jus can carry a 15% wine. Amarone's acidity cuts the mustard, and a bottle suits a table of two or more.

objections.q: "Amarone is a niche wine. Will anyone order it?"
objections.a: Guests know the name, and you have no Amarone for them to find. It also gives the floor a second answer at $165 when someone wants something big with the steak.

objections.q: "I already have Italian reds around $160 to $180."
objections.a: True. Frecciarossa Pinot Nero and Cordella Brunello sit close. Neither is a dried-grape wine, so the style differs, and the weight suits your two beef dishes better than a Pinot Nero does.

objections.q: "At 15% it is too heavy for lunch."
objections.a: Agreed, it is a dinner bottle. The $32 glass lets a single guest try it without opening a full bottle at the table.

a-677046.say: Your New World Cabernet starts at $460. Bishop Pine would sit at $70 with $13 by the glass, so a guest who wants California Cab with the steak has a place to land.

story.t: The sheet gives no tasting notes, so this is our estimate of what a California Cabernet Sauvignon is. Expect a full-bodied, dry red with blackcurrant, black cherry and some mocha, medium tannin, at 13% alcohol. The grape and the style are our estimate, not on the sheet.

Cabernet Sauvignon is the grape guests order by name, and California is the place they expect it from. Your list has Bordeaux Cabernet blends but no New World Cabernet under $460. A server can say it is the familiar steakhouse red at an easy price.

It is fruitier and softer than Château Camino Salva and Château Le Crock, which are Bordeaux with a drier, more savoury edge. Medium tannin suits grilled beef and a peppercorn sauce. It is lighter than the Brunello with the pappardelle, so it works with the braised beef cheek.

They pay $20.21 a bottle, $242.52 a case of 12. On the list it lands at $70, 3.5 times cost, level with Piattelli Alto Molino Malbec at $70 and just under Dissegna Pinot Nero at $75. By the glass it is $13, about $4.04 cost a pour from 5 pours. It is on consignment, with 22 cases in the warehouse.

dishes.d-beef-cheek-pappardelle: Rosemary and parmigiano with braised beef cheek want a dry red with some fruit and moderate tannin. This is a plainer, cheaper pour than the Cordella Brunello at $181.
dishes.d-42oz-cote-de-boeuf: The red wine and mustard jus needs a red with body. This is a straightforward option for a table that wants Cabernet without paying the $180 or more they ask now.

objections.q: "Your supply is only 22 cases. What if it runs out?"
objections.a: That is a real limit, and it is on consignment. At your volume it should last a while, but I would not build a feature around it.

objections.q: "I already have Malbec at $70 for the steak."
objections.a: You do, and it sells. This gives a guest who wants Cabernet by name something that is not Bordeaux. If Malbec covers it for you, that is a fair answer.

objections.q: "Is a $70 California Cab good enough for this room?"
objections.a: It is an easy, fruit-forward bottle, not a serious one. It sits at the entry point of your reds, and you keep the Bordeaux for guests who want more.

a-490896.say: Your four rosés come from the Rhône, Languedoc, Campania and Niagara, and none is from Provence. This one is, and it would sit at $115, above anything else pink on the list.

story.t: A pale, dry rosé from Côtes de Provence, mostly Grenache with Cinsault, Syrah and Mourvèdre. The sheet describes white peach, apricot and passion fruit on the nose, then a crunchy, fresh palate with citrus zest and a little cinnamon and cardamom. It is 12% alcohol and light in weight. Dry is our estimate, not on the sheet.

It is lighter and more fruit-led than the Aglianico Ros'Aura, and finer than the St. John Beausoleil, which is Syrah-heavy. The acidity and citrus note suit raw fish, shellfish and tomato dishes. The sheet itself points to scallops. It should be served cold, between 10 and 12°C.

They pay $34.95 a bottle, or $209.70 for a case of 6. On the list it lands at $115 a bottle, 3.3 times cost, and $22 a glass. That is well above St. John Beausoleil at $84, the next rosé down, so it works as the top pink rather than a rival to it. A glass is 5 pours a bottle at $6.99 cost a pour. Supply is LCBO stores only, Vintages, so nothing sits in the agency warehouse.

dishes.d-tuna-carpaccio: Ponzu and eggplant miso are salty and savoury. This rosé's citrus zest and crisp fruit lift raw tuna without covering it. It is lighter than the Ros'Aura you pour there now.
dishes.d-shrimp-linguine: Lemon, caper and tomato need acidity, and this wine has it. The 'nduja adds heat, and the peach and apricot fruit softens it. A lighter, fresher fit than the Ros'Aura.
dishes.d-roasted-cauliflower: Chili oil, pomegranate and labneh give sweet, sharp and creamy notes. The passion fruit and spice in this rosé meet them, where St. John Beausoleil is more savoury and herbal.
dishes.d-seared-rainbow-trout: Trout is delicate and the piquillo, olive and basil add salt and sweetness. A light, dry rosé keeps the fish in front. The sheet's pairing with salmon points the same way.

objections.q: "$115 is a lot for a rosé. My guests stop at $84."
objections.a: That is fair. St. John at $84 stays your value pink. This one is for the table that asks for Provence by name, and it gives you a clear step up.

objections.q: "I already have four rosés."
objections.a: You do, but none is from Provence. A guest who asks for it has nothing to order today. It would replace a gap, not repeat a wine.

objections.q: "It is a 2020. Is that too old for a rosé?"
objections.a: Rosé is usually drunk young, so it is worth a look at how it is showing. The sheet describes fresh fruit and crunch. I would ask for a taste before you list it.

a-616276.say: You list two large-format bottles, and no magnum of an Italian red like this one. At $160, it would sit beside the Masciarelli Montepulciano, which is also $160, so the list needs a reason to choose it.

story.t: A full-bodied dry red from Veneto, mostly Corvina with Rondinella and Molinara. The sheet describes ripe cherry, sweet spice and soft tannins with a long finish. It is 13.5% alcohol and sold in a 1.5L bottle. Medium tannin and dry are our estimate.

They pay $47.00 a bottle, or $282.00 for a case of 6. On the list it lands at $160 a bottle, 3.4 times cost. That matches Masciarelli Marina Cvetic at $160 and sits just under Domaine Roger Perrin Châteauneuf-du-Pape at $163. There are 309 cases in the warehouse, so supply is not a worry.

dishes.d-beef-cheek-pappardelle: Slow-cooked beef cheek is rich, and rosemary and parmigiano add savoury depth. The soft tannin and cherry fruit suit it, and cost far less than the Brunello you pour at $181.
dishes.d-10oz-steak-frites: Peppercorn sauce wants fruit and some weight without harsh tannin. This wine gives ripe cherry and spice, and a magnum suits a table sharing steaks. It is softer than the Le Crock.
dishes.d-42oz-cote-de-boeuf: A shared côte de boeuf with a red wine and mustard jus suits a big bottle. The 1.5L size feeds the table, and the dried-fruit richness stands up to the jus.

objections.q: "I already have bottles at $160 and $163. Why add another?"
objections.a: Concede the price is crowded. The difference is size. It is a 1.5L bottle for a big table, and nothing like it is on your list.

objections.q: "My two large formats are prestige names. Is this too humble?"
objections.a: It is a more everyday name, yes. It suits the table that wants to share a magnum with steak or pasta, not the collector. It fills a different need.

objections.q: "Will guests understand why a magnum costs $160?"
objections.a: A magnum holds two bottles, so the price per glass is modest. The double fermentation story gives the server something to say.
